About 750 kW of heat is released (≈ 2.7 GJ/h).

I worked this by hand and did not run any code. The arithmetic is short enough to check directly.

The −92 kJ is per mole of reaction as written, and one mole of reaction makes 2 mol of NH3. That gives 46 kJ released per mol of NH3.

- Molar flow of NH3: 1000 kg/h ÷ 17.031 kg/kmol = 58.72 kmol/h, which is 16.31 mol/s.
- Heat released: 16.31 mol/s × 46 kJ/mol = 750 kJ/s, which is 750 kW.

A common mistake is to treat −92 kJ as per mole of NH3. That doubles the answer to about 1500 kW.

This uses the standard ΔH at about 25 °C as given. At real converter conditions (around 400–500 °C) the heat of reaction is somewhat larger in magnitude, roughly −100 to −110 kJ per mol of reaction. I am recalling that figure from memory and did not compute it.
